cards.def: A late-medieval aristocratic narrative, in verse or prose, whose major themes concern love and its effects on human behavior, typically moving through social integration, disintegration by tests and marvels, and reintegration.
The medieval ideals of knighthood, including bravery, courtesy, honor, and gallantry toward women, whose essence in this poem is truth as proclaimed by the pentangle on Gawain's shield.
Refinement and behavior from good breeding, the courtly skills of temperance, reverence for women, and manners that a romance hero must add to valor, generosity, loyalty, honor, and skill in battle.
In fourteenth-century English, not only truthfulness but also "troth," fidelity pledged by one's word and owed to a lord, a spouse, or anyone to whom one has an obligation.
An ennobling love, often modeled on feudal service, in which a knight serves his lady with the obedience and loyalty he owes his liege lord, whether or not the love is consummated or returned.
A five-pointed star Solomon set as a token of fidelity, called in England the endless knot because each line overlaps and links with the last so the figure is ever eternal.
The English name for the pentangle, a five-pointed form that never fails, never stronger to one side or slack at the other, but unbroken from beginning to end.
The pentangle's meaning as the virtue the Green Knight tests, the fidelity Gawain's shield proclaims.

The five short rhyming lines (a b a b a) that close each stanza: a one-stress "bob" followed by a four-line "wheel" of three-stress lines (iambic trimeter in Armitage), per the Norton headnote, p. A-413.
The fourteenth-century Middle English return to long alliterative lines, the prosody of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight together with its bob and wheel.
The Green Knight's challenge that one stroke be struck and another returned after one year and one day, with the axe given to whoever accepts.
A bargain to swap daily gains so that what one party wins outdoors is traded for what the other gains indoors.
The opening transfer of empire that traces power from fallen Troy through Aeneas, Romulus, and Felix Brutus to Britain and Arthur.
An elaborate formal description of a person's appearance.

cards.term: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
cards.def: An Arthurian chivalric romance from the alliterative revival, considered a masterpiece of Middle English about knightly deeds, sexual enticement, and wild landscapes.
The evergreen sprig the Green Knight holds in one hand to show he means peace and no malice when he enters Arthur's hall.
The huge green-steel axe the Green Knight offers as the weapon of the Christmas game.
Arthur's fellowship of the most chivalrous and courteous knights known to Christendom, gathered at Camelot.
